lead: An adiabatic saturator is a chamber where air meets recirculated water with no heat through the walls. The air cools and takes up water vapour until it becomes saturated. The temperature it reaches is the adiabatic saturation temperature. A wet-bulb thermometer follows the same path: a wet wick cools until sensible heat from the air equals the latent heat of evaporation. Both give humidity from two temperatures, and both set the lower limit for evaporative cooling. They appear in cooling towers, air conditioning, dryer design and weather measurement.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.1 for humidity and enthalpy, and Chapter 7.2 for reading the chart.

blocks.text: An adiabatic saturator is a well-insulated chamber. Air enters with dry-bulb temperature T and humidity Y. It flows over a large water surface. The water is recirculated, so it stays at the temperature the air reaches. No external heat enters. Some water evaporates. The latent heat comes from the air, so the air cools. The air leaves saturated at the adiabatic saturation temperature T<sub>as</sub>. Its humidity is Y<sub>s</sub>(T<sub>as</sub>), the saturation humidity at that temperature.

blocks.where: Y is humidity of the entering air (kg water/kg dry air); T is dry-bulb temperature (°C); T<sub>as</sub> is adiabatic saturation temperature (°C); Y<sub>s</sub>(T<sub>as</sub>) is saturation humidity at T<sub>as</sub>; c<sub>s</sub> is humid heat ≈1.00+1.88Y kJ/(kg dry air·K); λ<sub>s</sub> is latent heat at T<sub>as</sub> (kJ/kg water).

blocks.text: The enthalpy balance says the sensible heat lost by the air equals the latent heat used to evaporate the water. On a chart of Y against T, this equation is a straight line with slope −c<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>s</sub>. The line starts at the known air state and ends on the saturation curve at T<sub>as</sub>. For air–water, λ<sub>s</sub> is about 2450 kJ/kg near room temperature, so the slope is about −0.00042 kg/kg per K. The line is nearly flat.

A wet-bulb thermometer has a bulb covered by a wet cloth wick. Air flows past the wick. Water evaporates from the wick. The wick cools below the air temperature. At steady state, sensible heat from the air to the wick equals latent heat carried away by evaporation.

blocks.where: h<sub>c</sub> is convective heat transfer coefficient (W/m²·K); T<sub>w</sub> is wet-bulb temperature (°C); k<sub>Y</sub> is mass transfer coefficient (kg/m²·s·ΔY); λ is latent heat at T<sub>w</sub> (J/kg water); Y<sub>s</sub>(T<sub>w</sub>) is saturation humidity at T<sub>w</sub>; Y is humidity of the air.

blocks.text: For a reliable reading, keep the wick wet, keep air speed above about 3 m/s, and shield the wick from radiation. Low air speed or a dry wick gives a reading closer to the dry-bulb temperature.

The Lewis relation for air–water is h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub>c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1, in consistent units. Put this into the wet-bulb equation and it becomes the same adiabatic saturation equation. So T<sub>w</sub> ≈ T<sub>as</sub> for air–water. For organic vapours the Lewis relation does not hold, so wet-bulb temperature and adiabatic saturation temperature are different.

sections.h3: Reading humidity and the cooling limit

blocks.text: On the chart, start at the saturation curve at T<sub>w</sub>. Move along the adiabatic line to the dry-bulb temperature T. Read Y at the air state. For T = 40 °C and T<sub>w</sub> = 22 °C, Y<sub>s</sub>(22) = 0.0167 kg/kg and the line gives Y ≈ 0.0092 kg/kg dry air. Only two temperatures are needed.

The wet-bulb temperature is the lower limit of adiabatic cooling for air–water. Air can cool toward Tw by evaporating water into it, but not below Tw in that process. In a cooling tower the water outlet approaches the entering air wet-bulb temperature, not its dry-bulb temperature; see Chapter 7.5.

figure.caption: The worked example. Air at 40 °C with Y = 0.0092 cools along its adiabatic saturation line, slope −c<sub>s</sub>/λ ≈ −0.00042 per K, until it meets the saturation curve at 22 °C with Y = 0.0167. For air–water this end point is also the wet-bulb temperature. The dew point of the same air, 12.7 °C, lies on the horizontal through the start.

spec.aria: Psychrometric chart from 10 to 45 degrees. A straight sloping line runs from the air state at 40 degrees and humidity 0.0092 up to the saturation curve at 22 degrees and 0.0167. A dashed horizontal from the air state meets saturation at the dew point, 12.7 degrees.

examples.question: Air at 40 °C dry bulb and 20 % relative humidity has Y = 0.0092 kg/kg dry air. It passes a wet-bulb thermometer and then an adiabatic saturator. Find the wet-bulb temperature and the humidity after the saturator.
steps: Entering humidity is given: Y = 0.0092 kg/kg dry air. A check from 20 % relative humidity at 40 °C gives the same value.
Try T<sub>w</sub> = 22 °C. The saturation humidity at 22 °C is Y<sub>s</sub>(22) = 0.0167 kg/kg dry air.
This matches the entering 0.0092, so the wet-bulb and adiabatic saturation temperature is T<sub>w</sub> ≈ 22 °C.
In an ideal saturator the air leaves saturated at 22 °C, so Y<sub>out</sub> = Y<sub>s</sub>(22) = 0.0167 kg/kg dry air.
Water gained = 0.0167 − 0.0092 = 0.0075 kg water per kg dry air.
examples.answer: The wet-bulb temperature is about 22 °C, the air leaves at Y = 0.0167 kg/kg dry air, and it gains 0.0075 kg water per kg dry air.
examples.check:
import math
T=40.0
RH=0.20
P=101.325
psat40=0.6113*math.exp(17.27*T/(T+237.3))
pw=RH*psat40
Y=0.622*pw/(P-pw)
Tw=22.0
psatw=0.6113*math.exp(17.27*Tw/(Tw+237.3))
Ys=0.622*psatw/(P-psatw)
print(round(Tw,1))
print(round(Ys,4))
print(round(Ys-Y,4))

traps: Writing wet-bulb temperature equal to adiabatic saturation temperature for every vapour. They are equal only for air–water, where the Lewis relation holds.
Using the dry-bulb temperature instead of T<sub>w</sub> or T<sub>as</sub> when finding Y<sub>s</sub>. The saturation humidity must be taken at the wet-bulb or adiabatic saturation temperature.
Mixing units: λ is in kJ/kg while c<sub>s</sub> is in kJ/(kg·K). Using λ in J/kg without converting the other term gives a factor-of-1000 error.
Forgetting the practical conditions. A dry wick, low air speed or strong radiation makes the wet-bulb reading unreliable.
Getting the sign wrong on the adiabatic line. As T falls, Y rises, so the slope is negative: −c<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Define adiabatic saturation temperature in one sentence.
quiz.a: It is the temperature reached by air that contacts recirculated water adiabatically until the air becomes saturated.

quiz.q: Why does air cool in an adiabatic saturator?
quiz.a: Evaporation takes latent heat from the air. No external heat replaces it, so the sensible heat of the air falls and its temperature drops.

quiz.q: Air at 30 °C with Y = 0.010 kg/kg passes over a wet wick that reads 20 °C. Check whether 20 °C is the right wet-bulb temperature for this air, using Ys(20) = 0.0147, cs = 1.02 kJ/(kg·K) and λ = 2450 kJ/kg.
quiz.a: The wet-bulb line through 20 °C gives Y = 0.0147 − (1.02/2450)(30 − 20) = 0.0147 − 0.0042 = 0.0105 kg/kg. The air holds 0.010, slightly less, so its true wet-bulb temperature is a little below 20 °C, about 19.6 °C. The reading is good to within half a degree.

quiz.q: Why is T<sub>w</sub> = T<sub>as</sub> not true for organic vapours?
quiz.a: The equality needs the Lewis relation h<sub>c</sub>/(k<sub>Y</sub>c<sub>s</sub>) ≈ 1. Many organic vapours have different heat and mass transfer behaviour, so the two temperatures differ.

quiz.q: Air at T = 35 °C has T<sub>w</sub> = 25 °C, Y<sub>s</sub>(25) = 0.0200, c<sub>s</sub> = 1.04 kJ/(kg·K), λ = 2440 kJ/kg. Find Y.
Explain why wet-bulb temperature is the lower limit of adiabatic cooling.
quiz.a: As the air cools by evaporating water, its humidity rises along the adiabatic line. At Tw the air is saturated, so it can take no more vapour, no more latent heat can be drawn from it, and the cooling stops. Evaporation alone cannot take the air or the water below Tw.

quiz.q: List three conditions for a reliable wet-bulb reading.
quiz.a: Wick kept wet, air speed above about 3 m/s, and radiation shield.

beyond: Not for the exam. In HVAC, wet-bulb temperature sets the load on evaporative coolers and the limit of comfort cooling. In cooling-tower testing, the approach to wet bulb is the performance number. In drying, the wet-bulb line tells how far air can pick up moisture before it saturates. The Lewis relation links heat and mass transfer coefficients in correlated form. Search next for 'psychrometric chart', 'Lewis relation', and 'cooling tower approach'.
